gr.about: Greece sits at the southern tip of the Balkans, a mountainous mainland fringed by thousands of islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas. About 10 million people speak Greek in a parliamentary republic. Its ancient city-states invented democracy, philosophy and the Olympics; Alexander spread Greek culture across the Near East before Rome and then Byzantium absorbed it. Nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule ended with the war of independence in the 1820s. A turbulent 20th century brought monarchy, civil war and a military junta before stable democracy, EU membership and a painful debt crisis in the 2010s.
known: Islands such as Santorini and Crete

gl.about: Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark and the world's largest island, lying between the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. An ice sheet covers about four fifths of it, so its roughly 57,000 people, mostly Inuit, live in coastal towns and speak Greenlandic and Danish. Norse settlers arrived around 986 and vanished by the 15th century; Danish colonisation began in 1721. Greenland became an integral part of Denmark in 1953, won home rule in 1979, left the European Community in 1985 and gained expanded self-government in 2009. Denmark still handles defence and foreign affairs.
dates: Erik the Red founds Norse settlements
Becomes part of the Kingdom of Denmark

gd.about: Grenada is a small volcanic island nation at the southern end of the Caribbean's Windward Islands, with about 125,000 English-speaking people. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Colonised by the French in the 17th century and ceded to Britain in 1763, it became independent in 1974. A 1979 left-wing revolution ended in 1983 when its leader was killed in an internal coup, prompting a US-led invasion. Nicknamed the Spice Isle, it is a major producer of nutmeg and mace and relies heavily on tourism.
dates: Revolution brings Maurice Bishop to power
known: Nutmeg and the Spice Isle nickname

gu.about: Guam is an unincorporated territory of the United States, the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands in the western Pacific. Its roughly 170,000 people, including the indigenous Chamorro, are US citizens who speak English and Chamorro but cannot vote for president. Spain claimed the island after Magellan's 1521 visit and ruled it until ceding it to the United States in 1898. Japan occupied Guam during the Second World War before US forces retook it in 1944. The 1950 Organic Act granted civilian government, and large US naval and air bases remain central to the economy alongside tourism.

gt.about: Guatemala is the most populous country in Central America, with about 18 million people, lying south of Mexico between the Pacific and the Caribbean. Spanish is official but over twenty Mayan languages are spoken, and nearly half the population is indigenous. The heartland of ancient Maya civilisation, it was conquered by Spain in 1524 and became independent in 1821. A US-backed coup in 1954 toppled a reformist government and helped trigger a 36-year civil war that killed some 200,000 people, mostly Maya. Peace accords in 1996 restored civilian democracy, though poverty and corruption persist.
dates: Peace accords end the civil war

gg.about: Guernsey is a British Crown Dependency in the Channel Islands, close to the Normandy coast of France. It is not part of the United Kingdom or the EU: it governs itself through the States of Guernsey while the UK handles defence and foreign affairs. About 64,000 people live there, speaking English, with a fading Norman French dialect. Part of the Duchy of Normandy when William conquered England in 1066, it stayed loyal to the English crown after Normandy was lost in 1204. German forces occupied the island from 1940 to 1945. Finance is the main industry alongside tourism.
dates: Part of Normandy under William the Conqueror
known: Castle Cornet and St Peter Port harbour

gn.about: Guinea lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, with about 14 million people. French is the official language alongside Fula, Malinke and Susu, and most people are Muslim. It is a presidential republic with a history of coups. Once part of the Mali Empire, it became a French colony in the 1890s and in 1958 was the only French territory to vote for immediate independence. Sékou Touré ruled as a one-party dictator until 1984, followed by Lansana Conté until 2008 and further military takeovers, most recently in 2021. Guinea holds the world's largest bauxite reserves.
dates: Military coup after Sékou Touré's death

gw.about: Guinea-Bissau is a small, low-lying country on the West African coast between Senegal and Guinea, including the Bijagós archipelago. About 2 million people speak Portuguese officially and Crioulo in daily life. Formerly part of the Kaabu kingdom and then a Portuguese colony, it fought a guerrilla war from 1963 under Amílcar Cabral and won independence in 1974. Since then it has suffered repeated coups, a civil war in 1998 and 1999, and chronic instability; no elected president completed a full term until 2014. It is one of the world's poorest countries, dependent on cashew nuts.
dates: Coup brings João Vieira to power

gy.about: Guyana sits on the northeast coast of South America, the continent's only English-speaking country, with about 800,000 people of mostly Indian and African descent. Dense rainforest covers most of the interior while almost everyone lives on the coastal plain. Dutch colonies passed to Britain in 1814 and became British Guiana; independence came in 1966 and a republic in 1970. Politics has long split along ethnic lines. Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, two thirds of the country. Vast offshore oil finds since 2015 have made Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies.

ht.about: Haiti occupies the western third of Hispaniola in the Caribbean, with about 11.5 million people speaking Haitian Creole and French. As the French colony of Saint-Domingue it was the richest sugar colony in the world, worked by enslaved Africans. Their revolt from 1791 produced in 1804 the first independent Black republic and the only successful slave revolution. Crippling reparations to France, US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorships and repeated coups left it the poorest country in the Americas. A 2010 earthquake killed well over 100,000 people, and since the 2021 assassination of the president gangs have controlled much of the capital.

hn.about: Honduras lies in the middle of Central America with a long Caribbean coast and a short Pacific one, home to about 10.5 million Spanish-speaking people. The Maya city of Copán flourished here before Spanish conquest in the 1520s. Independent from 1821 and briefly part of a Central American federation, it became the archetypal banana republic in the 20th century, dominated by US fruit companies. It fought the brief Football War with El Salvador in 1969, was devastated by Hurricane Mitch in 1998, and saw a coup in 2009. Gang violence and poverty drive heavy emigration.

hk.about: Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China on the south coast, a dense city of about 7.5 million people speaking Cantonese and English. Britain took Hong Kong Island after the First Opium War in 1842, added Kowloon in 1860 and leased the New Territories for 99 years in 1898. It grew into a global financial hub and returned to China in 1997 under the one country, two systems principle, keeping its own legal system, currency and freedoms for 50 years. Mass protests in 2019 were followed by a 2020 national security law that sharply curtailed political dissent.
dates: Ceded to Britain after the Opium War
known: Dim sum and cha chaan teng cafés
Kung fu cinema and Bruce Lee

hu.about: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe on the Danube plain, with about 9.6 million people speaking Hungarian, a Uralic language unrelated to its neighbours. It is a parliamentary republic and EU member. Magyar tribes settled the Carpathian Basin in 895 and Stephen I founded a Christian kingdom in 1000. Ottoman defeat at Mohács split the kingdom, Habsburg rule followed, and the 1867 compromise created Austria-Hungary. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon stripped two thirds of its territory. Soviet tanks crushed the 1956 uprising; communism ended in 1989, and the country joined the EU in 2004.

is.about: Iceland is a volcanic island nation in the North Atlantic just below the Arctic Circle, with about 390,000 people speaking Icelandic, a language close to Old Norse. It is a parliamentary republic. Norse settlers arrived around 874 and in 930 founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland came under Norwegian and then Danish rule for centuries, gained sovereignty in 1918 and became a fully independent republic in 1944. Fishing, geothermal and hydro power, and tourism drive the economy, which collapsed spectacularly in the 2008 banking crisis before recovering.
dates: Becomes a sovereign state under Denmark

in.about: India occupies most of the South Asian subcontinent, stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. With about 1.4 billion people it is the world's most populous country and its largest democracy, a federal parliamentary republic with Hindi, English and twenty other official languages. Civilisation here dates to the Indus Valley around 2500 BC; empires such as the Maurya, Gupta and Mughal followed. Britain ruled directly from 1858 until 1947, when independence came with the traumatic partition that created Pakistan. Economic liberalisation after 1991 turned it into a major technology and services power.

id.about: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago, some 17,000 islands stretching along the equator between the Indian and Pacific oceans. With about 280 million people it is the fourth most populous country and the largest Muslim-majority one, united by the Indonesian language in a presidential republic. Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit preceded Islam; the Dutch dominated from the 17th century as the Dutch East Indies. Independence was proclaimed in 1945 after Japanese occupation and recognised in 1949. Suharto's authoritarian New Order lasted from the mid-1960s until 1998, when democracy returned.
dates: Mass killings bring Suharto to power
known: Volcanoes along the Ring of Fire

ir.about: Iran, historically Persia, is a large, mountainous country in western Asia between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf, with about 89 million people speaking Persian. It is an Islamic republic in which an unelected Supreme Leader holds ultimate power. Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BC, and Persian empires rose and fell for over a millennium before the Arab conquest brought Islam. The Safavids made Shia Islam the state religion in 1501. The 1979 revolution overthrew the Shah, and a devastating war with Iraq, sanctions and nuclear tensions have defined the decades since.

iq.about: Iraq lies in western Asia around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the ancient Mesopotamia where writing, cities and law codes first appeared. About 45 million people speak Arabic and Kurdish; most are Shia Muslims, with large Sunni Arab and Kurdish minorities. Baghdad was the glittering Abbasid capital from 762 until the Mongols sacked it in 1258. After Ottoman rule and a British mandate, a kingdom was founded in 1932 and overthrown in 1958. Saddam Hussein's dictatorship brought wars with Iran and Kuwait, the 2003 US-led invasion toppled him, and years of insurgency and the rise of ISIS followed.

ie.about: Ireland occupies most of an island on the western edge of Europe, with about 5.2 million people speaking English and, in some areas, Irish. It is a parliamentary republic and EU member; Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom. Celtic and Christian from early times, it fell under English control from the 12th century and was absorbed into the United Kingdom in 1801. The Great Famine of the 1840s killed a million and sent millions more abroad. The 1916 Easter Rising led to the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949. The 1998 Good Friday Agreement brought peace to the north.
dates: Act of Union with Great Britain
known: Cliffs of Moher and green landscapes

im.about: The Isle of Man is a British Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea between England and Ireland. It is self-governing and not part of the United Kingdom or the EU; the UK handles defence and foreign affairs. About 85,000 people live there, speaking English, with the Manx Gaelic language revived in recent decades. Its parliament, Tynwald, dates from Norse rule over a thousand years ago and claims to be the oldest in continuous existence. The island passed from Norway to Scotland and England, and the British crown bought out its lords in 1765. Offshore finance and e-gaming now dominate the economy.
dates: Norway cedes the island to Scotland
Stanley family become Lords of Man

il.about: Israel is a small country on the eastern Mediterranean, with about 9.9 million people, mostly Jewish with a large Arab minority, speaking Hebrew and Arabic. It is a parliamentary democracy with a strong technology economy. The Zionist movement sought a Jewish homeland from the 1890s; Britain's Balfour Declaration and the Palestine mandate followed. Israel declared independence in 1948 and was immediately at war with its Arab neighbours, and it captured the West Bank, Gaza, Golan and Sinai in 1967. Jerusalem is claimed as capital by both Israel and the Palestinians, and the conflict with the Palestinians remains unresolved.

it.about: Italy is a boot-shaped peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean from the Alps, plus Sicily and Sardinia, with about 59 million Italian-speaking people in a parliamentary republic. Rome ruled an empire spanning the ancient world; after its fall the peninsula split into city-states, kingdoms and papal lands that produced the Renaissance. Italy was unified in 1861 and gained Rome as capital in 1871. Mussolini's fascist regime led it into the Second World War; voters chose a republic in 1946 and Italy helped found the European Community. It remains a global centre of art, design, fashion and food.

ci.about: Ivory Coast, officially Côte d'Ivoire, lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, with about 30 million people. French is official among some sixty local languages. Abidjan is the economic capital while Yamoussoukro, birthplace of first president Félix Houphouët-Boigny, became the official capital in 1983. A French colony from 1893, it gained independence in 1960 and prospered under Houphouët-Boigny's long rule as the world's largest cocoa producer. After his death in 1993 came a coup, a north-south civil war and a disputed 2010 election that ended in fighting; stability and growth have since returned.
known: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace

jm.about: Jamaica is the third-largest Caribbean island, south of Cuba, with about 2.8 million people speaking English and Jamaican Patois. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. The Taíno lived here before Spain claimed it in 1494; England seized it in 1655 and built a sugar economy on slavery, which was abolished in the 1830s. Independence came in 1962. Despite its size, Jamaica's cultural reach is enormous: reggae and Bob Marley, Rastafari, dancehall, and sprinters like Usain Bolt. Tourism, bauxite and remittances sustain an economy troubled by debt and violent crime.
dates: Columbus claims the island for Spain

jp.about: Japan is an archipelago of four main islands and thousands of smaller ones off the east coast of Asia, with about 124 million people speaking Japanese. It is a constitutional monarchy with the world's oldest hereditary monarchy and a parliamentary government. Imperial courts at Nara and Kyoto gave way to centuries of samurai rule under shoguns, with the Tokugawa closing the country to the outside world from the 1630s. The 1868 Meiji Restoration launched rapid modernisation and imperial expansion that ended in defeat in 1945. Postwar Japan became a pacifist democracy and the world's second-largest economy by the 1980s.

je.about: Jersey is the largest of the Channel Islands and a British Crown Dependency, lying just off the coast of Normandy. Self-governing through its States Assembly, it is not part of the United Kingdom or the EU; the UK is responsible for defence and foreign relations. About 105,000 people live there, speaking English, with the Norman French dialect Jèrriais surviving among a few. Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933, it stayed with the English crown when Normandy was lost in 1204. German troops occupied it from 1940 to 1945. Finance dominates the economy, with Jersey Royal potatoes, dairy cattle and tourism alongside.
dates: Becomes part of the Duchy of Normandy
Remains loyal to the English crown

jo.about: Jordan is a mostly desert country in the Middle East, landlocked except for a short Red Sea coast at Aqaba, with about 11 million Arabic-speaking people including millions of Palestinian and Syrian refugees. It is a constitutional monarchy ruled by the Hashemite dynasty, which claims descent from the Prophet Muhammad. Home to the Nabataean city of Petra, the land was long an Ottoman backwater before Britain created the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. Independent since 1946, Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950 and lost it to Israel in 1967, then signed peace with Israel in 1994. It is a stable Western ally in a volatile region.
dates: Loses the West Bank in Six-Day War

kz.about: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country and ninth largest overall, stretching across Central Asian steppe from the Caspian Sea to China. About 20 million people speak Kazakh and Russian in a presidential republic dominated for three decades by Nursultan Nazarbayev. Nomadic Kazakh khanates emerged in the 15th century before Russian conquest in the 18th and 19th centuries; Soviet collectivisation caused a devastating famine in the 1930s. Independent since 1991, it moved its capital from Almaty to Astana in 1997 and grew rich on oil, gas and uranium. Russia's Baikonur Cosmodrome still launches rockets from its steppe.

ke.about: Kenya straddles the equator on the east coast of Africa, from Indian Ocean beaches through highlands and the Rift Valley to Lake Victoria. About 55 million people from over forty ethnic groups speak Swahili and English in a presidential republic. Swahili trading cities lined the coast for centuries before Britain made it a protectorate in 1895 and a settler colony. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s hastened independence in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta; Daniel arap Moi ruled for 24 years. Deadly post-election violence in 2007 led to a new constitution in 2010. Kenya is East Africa's economic hub and a safari destination.
known: Mount Kenya and the Rift Valley

ki.about: Kiribati is a Pacific island nation of 33 coral atolls scattered across an ocean area the size of India, straddling the equator and spanning three island groups. About 130,000 people speak Gilbertese and English in a parliamentary republic. Britain made the Gilbert Islands a protectorate in 1892; the 1943 Battle of Tarawa was among the bloodiest of the Pacific war. Independence came in 1979. In 1995 Kiribati shifted the date line so the whole country shares one day, making it the first to see each new year. With most land barely two metres above sea level, it is among the countries most threatened by rising seas.
dates: Gilbert Islands become a British protectorate
known: First country to see the new year
Low-lying atolls threatened by sea rise

xk.about: Kosovo is a small landlocked country in the Balkans, with about 1.7 million people, overwhelmingly ethnic Albanian with a Serb minority, speaking Albanian and Serbian in a parliamentary republic. Medieval Serbian kingdoms and the 1389 Battle of Kosovo give it deep significance for Serbs; centuries of Ottoman rule followed before Serbia took it in 1912. It was an autonomous province of Yugoslavia until Milošević revoked that status in 1989. A 1998-99 war ended with NATO bombing and UN administration. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; it is recognised by around 100 countries but not by Serbia, Russia or China, and its status remains disputed.
dates: Battle of Kosovo against the Ottomans
Serbia takes Kosovo from the Ottomans
known: Pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora's heritage

kw.about: Kuwait is a small, flat desert state at the head of the Persian Gulf, wedged between Iraq and Saudi Arabia. About 4.5 million people live there, but only around a third are citizens; the rest are foreign workers. Arabic is official and the country is an emirate ruled by the Al-Sabah family since the 18th century, with an elected parliament that is unusually assertive for the Gulf. A British protectorate from 1899, it became independent in 1961. Oil, discovered in 1938, made it among the world's richest countries per head. Iraq's 1990 invasion was reversed by a US-led coalition in the 1991 Gulf War.

kg.about: Kyrgyzstan is a landlocked, overwhelmingly mountainous country in Central Asia, dominated by the Tian Shan range and the vast alpine Lake Issyk-Kul. About 7 million people speak Kyrgyz and Russian in a parliamentary-presidential republic, the most politically open in the region though prone to upheaval. Nomadic Kyrgyz tribes came under Russian rule in the 1870s and became a Soviet republic in 1936. Since independence in 1991, popular uprisings toppled presidents in 2005 and 2010. Gold mining, remittances and herding sustain a poor economy; yurts, horses and the Manas epic poem anchor national identity.

la.about: Laos is a landlocked, mountainous country in Southeast Asia along the Mekong River, with about 7.6 million people speaking Lao. It is one of the world's few remaining one-party communist states. The kingdom of Lan Xang, the Land of a Million Elephants, was founded in 1353; the French made Laos a protectorate in 1893. Independent from 1953, it was engulfed by the Vietnam War, becoming the most heavily bombed country per person in history, with unexploded ordnance still a danger. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975. Hydropower, mining and tourism to temple-filled Luang Prabang drive a growing economy.

lv.about: Latvia is a flat, forested country on the Baltic Sea between Estonia and Lithuania, with about 1.9 million people speaking Latvian and a large Russian-speaking minority. It is a parliamentary republic and member of the EU and NATO. German crusaders founded Riga in 1201 and ruled through the Livonian Order; Poland, Sweden and then Russia from 1721 followed. Latvia declared independence in 1918, was annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, and regained freedom in 1991 after the peaceful Singing Revolution and the Baltic Way human chain. It joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014.

lb.about: Lebanon is a small, mountainous country on the eastern Mediterranean, bordered by Syria and Israel, with about 5.5 million people speaking Arabic, plus French and English. It has an unusual power-sharing system dividing top offices among Christians, Sunnis and Shia. Phoenician cities such as Tyre and Byblos traded across the ancient world. After Ottoman rule and a French mandate, independence came in 1943. A civil war from 1975 to 1990 drew in Syria, Israel and the Palestinians, and Hezbollah fought Israel in 2006. Since 2019 a catastrophic financial collapse and the 2020 Beirut port explosion have deepened the crisis.
known: Phoenician heritage of Byblos and Tyre

ls.about: Lesotho is a small, mountainous kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, the only country in the world lying wholly above 1,000 metres. About 2.3 million people speak Sesotho and English in a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary government. King Moshoeshoe I united the Basotho in the 1820s and sought British protection in 1868 to fend off Boer settlers; the colony of Basutoland became independent in 1966. Politics has been marked by coups and disputed elections. Water sold to South Africa, diamonds, textiles and remittances from miners support a poor economy, and HIV rates are among the world's highest.
known: Pony trekking in the Maloti mountains

lr.about: Liberia lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa between Sierra Leone and Ivory Coast, with about 5.5 million people speaking English and many local languages. Africa's oldest republic, it was founded by freed Black Americans resettled from 1822 by the American Colonization Society and declared independence in 1847. The settler elite dominated until a 1980 coup by Samuel Doe, and two civil wars between 1989 and 2003 killed around 250,000 people. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female head of state in 2006, and footballer George Weah succeeded her in 2018. Rubber, iron ore and ship registration anchor the economy.
dates: Samuel Doe seizes power in coup

ly.about: Libya is a large, mostly Saharan country on North Africa's Mediterranean coast, with about 7 million Arabic-speaking people clustered along the shore. Greeks, Romans and Phoenicians left spectacular ruins at Cyrene, Leptis Magna and Sabratha. Ottoman rule gave way to brutal Italian colonisation in 1911 and independence as a kingdom in 1951. Muammar Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled eccentrically for 42 years on oil wealth until the 2011 uprising and NATO intervention ended with his death. Rival governments in the east and west have fought intermittently since 2014, and the country remains divided and unstable.

li.about: Liechtenstein is a tiny Alpine principality wedged between Switzerland and Austria along the Rhine, one of only two doubly landlocked countries. About 40,000 German-speaking people live there under a constitutional monarchy in which the prince retains unusually strong powers, confirmed by a 2003 referendum. The Liechtenstein family bought the territory and had it made a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719; it became sovereign in 1806. It abolished its army in 1868, entered a customs union with Switzerland in 1923 and uses the Swiss franc. Banking, precision manufacturing and low taxes make it one of the richest countries per head.
dates: Becomes a principality of the Holy Roman Empire
known: Vaduz Castle, home of the prince
Dental products maker Ivoclar and Hilti tools
